planting.note: Start seed indoors or plant divisions/nursery starts after frost danger passes; give it a sturdy trellis or arbor since the twining vine can reach 20+ feet once established.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil against a strong trellis, fence, or arbor, since this vigorous twining vine can climb 20 feet or more in a season once mature. The tuberous roots, harvested at three to four years or older, are the part traditionally processed and used in Chinese herbalism, most often after steaming with black beans; fresh raw root is generally considered unsuitable for casual use. Grown ornamentally for its glossy heart-shaped leaves and airy sprays of small white flowers in late summer, it tolerates a range of soils but appreciates consistent moisture while establishing. Cut back hard in late winter to control size, as unmanaged vines can become congested and woody at the base.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Start seed indoors in late winter and transplant into rich, well-drained soil after frost; roots are typically dug for use in autumn of the second growing year.

directions: Sow in a loose, humus-rich, well-drained bed in partial shade with protection from harsh afternoon sun, as this thistle-like aster relative resents soggy or heavy clay soil. Foliage is coarse and somewhat ornamental with purplish thistle-type flower heads in late summer, but the plant is grown almost entirely for its aromatic, camphor-scented rhizome, dug in fall of the second or third year for traditional use in Chinese herbal preparations. Mulch to keep roots cool and moist through summer, and divide or replant offsets in early spring to keep a patch productive. Because it is slow to establish from seed, many gardeners start with purchased rhizome divisions instead.

planting.note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost and transplant into rich, well-worked soil once nights stay above 45°F; roots are dug in fall for processing.

directions: Grow in loose, deeply worked, fertile soil so the thick tuberous roots can expand without obstruction, and site in full sun to light afternoon shade in hotter climates. The plant forms a low rosette of hairy, wrinkled leaves and sends up spikes of tubular reddish-purple flowers reminiscent of foxglove, its distant relative. Fresh root or steamed, dried root is the part used in traditional Chinese herbalism, and mature roots are typically harvested in autumn after two full growing seasons. Keep soil evenly moist but not waterlogged, and mulch in colder zones since the crown can be marginally hardy where winters are severe.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Seed needs a cold stratification period before it will germinate reliably, so sow in containers and chill for 4-6 weeks or start outdoors in fall; plants take several years to reach flowering and harvestable root size.

directions: Sow stratified seed in deep, well-drained, humus-rich soil, since this long-lived alpine meadow perennial forms a substantial taproot and resents being moved once established. Broad ribbed leaves form a large basal clump for the first several years before the plant sends up tall stalks of striking whorled yellow flowers, usually not before its third or fourth season. The intensely bitter root, harvested only after many years of growth, is a classic European digestive bitter used in traditional tonics and liqueurs; commercial harvest generally waits until plants are at least four to ten years old. Give it cool summers, good winter drainage, and full sun to light shade, as it struggles in hot, humid climates.

planting.note: Start seed indoors in late winter and transplant into a sunny, well-drained bed or large container once soil has warmed; in cold-winter regions grow it as a container plant brought indoors for winter or replanted annually.

directions: Plant in loose, sandy, well-drained soil and provide a trellis or nearby shrub for the scrambling, thorny stems to climb, as this relative of garden asparagus can sprawl or vine several feet. Fine feathery foliage and small white flowers give way to red berries, but the plant is grown primarily for its clustered tuberous roots, traditionally harvested at one to two years and used in Ayurvedic tonics. It is frost-tender and best treated as a container specimen or annual outside zones 9-11, overwintered indoors in a bright spot where winters are cold. Keep soil evenly moist during the growing season and reduce watering once roots go dormant in cooler months.

planting.note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in early spring, or in fall in mild-winter climates for earlier bloom; succession sow every few weeks to keep flowers coming through the aphid season.

directions: Scatter seed directly over prepared soil in a sunny spot, tucking it along vegetable bed borders and pathways where its low, spreading habit will not shade neighboring crops. The white-and-yellow, egg-yolk-centered flowers bloom prolifically for weeks and are one of the most reliable draws for hoverflies, whose aphid-eating larvae make this a favorite in organic vegetable gardens. It thrives in cool weather and tends to fade or stop flowering once summer heat arrives, so many gardeners treat it as an early-spring and fall companion planting rather than a summer-long bloomer. Deadheading lightly extends bloom, but it also self-seeds readily and will often return on its own the following year.
sources: University of California Statewide IPM Program
